extracted.intended_audience: interest groups, regulatory advocates, and researchers studying public comments and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing public comments on federal agency rules so they are more likely to influence agency decisions, based on empirical findings about which comment features predict policy influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-coalition consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment cite or align with positions from typically opposed stakeholders to demonstrate consensus?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McKay & Yackee find that when multiple comments from different sectors (industry, NGOs, states, academics) converge on the same recommendation, agencies move. Effective comments cite or reference allied positions across diverse stakeholders to demonstrate consensus and reduce agency skepticism about one-sided advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original substantive content (not form-letter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment differ substantively from form-letter language and contribute unique content?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form letters and mass campaigns generally fail to alter policy because they have low informational value. A high-quality individual comment that provides unique factual, analytical, or experiential material is more powerful than many identical form letters. Ensure the submission contains substantive argumentation or evidence rather than boilerplate phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds new information to the agency record
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment provide information the agency does not already possess?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information content drives agency responsiveness: effective comments include unique factual, analytical, or experiential content that the agency could not have obtained otherwise. Prioritize supplying new data, concrete examples, original analysis, or firsthand experiences that fill gaps in the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part of a diverse, coordinated coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the comment part of a coordinated diverse coalition rather than a single-sector campaign?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that are part of a coordinated, cross-sector coalition (rather than isolated submissions from a single sector) are more likely to influence agencies. Single-sector campaigns face more agency skepticism; coordination that shows support from a range of stakeholders increases credibility and persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate breadth of support
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comment articulate the breadth of support for its position (geographic, sectoral, ideological)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly describing the scope of backing—e.g., geographic diversity, participation by multiple sectors, or support across ideological lines—helps demonstrate consensus and the broader significance of the recommendation. Cite allied organizations, jurisdictions, or stakeholder types to communicate this breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mass/form-letter campaigns (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the submission individualized and informative rather than part of a mass-produced campaign of identical letters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: McKay & Yackee confirm earlier findings that mass comment campaigns from individuals tend to have low informational content and elicit little direct policy response. Treat form-letter campaigns as an anti-pattern: they may show volume but rarely provide the distinct information agencies use to change rules.
